lines.text: Imagine a machine that can create money out of thin air.
Not counterfeit money. Real, brand-new dollars.
Now, if a million of those dollars came out tomorrow,
would it matter who got them first?
It turns out, it matters a lot.
It may be why your rent keeps climbing, why your savings seem to shrink, and why the people at the top keep pulling further ahead.
It's called the Cantillon Effect.
Three hundred years ago in Paris, a banker named Richard Cantillon had a front-row seat to a wild experiment.
France had started printing paper money like never before. Cantillon made a fortune, and he noticed something most people missed.
New money doesn't spread through an economy evenly. It enters at one specific point, and ripples outward.
Picture a drop falling into a still pond.
The water closest to the splash moves first. The far shore feels it last.
With money, the ripple is rising prices. And where you stand in that pond changes everything.
Let's shrink it down to a tiny town, where a loaf of bread costs one dollar.
One day, a stack of new money is created, and handed to one person: the banker. He's first in line.
He spends it right away, hiring builders and buying property, all at yesterday's prices.
The builder he hires gets that money next. With more money chasing the same goods, prices start to creep up. But her pay went up first, so she barely notices.
Then the money reaches the shopkeeper. Business is booming, so bread now costs a dollar fifty.
And the teacher and the retiree? Their incomes haven't changed at all. But bread now costs two dollars.
Nobody stole anything. Nobody broke the law.
And yet, wealth quietly moved, from the people at the back of the line, to the people at the front.
Now, scale that up to today's world.
Modern money is created by central banks, and by commercial banks every time they make a loan.
The first to touch it are banks, governments, and big investors, who can borrow cheaply and buy assets, like stocks and real estate, before prices move.
So asset prices tend to rise first. Then the money trickles into businesses, and eventually, into wages. Wages are almost always last.
In twenty twenty, trillions of new dollars were created. Within months, the stock market hit record highs.
A year later, groceries and rent started to climb. And wages? For two years, they fell behind prices.
So what does this mean for you?
If you earn a paycheck, you're usually near the back of the line. Your raise tends to arrive after prices have already moved.
If you save in cash, its value slowly leaks away. It's like walking up an escalator that's going down.
And if you don't own a home yet, it can run away from you faster than you can save for it.
Meanwhile, people who already own assets, and who sit closest to the source, get richer without doing anything differently.
That's how the gap grows.
The Cantillon Effect isn't a conspiracy. It's simply how new money moves. But because it's invisible, most people never notice it.
Inflation isn't just prices going up. It's a transfer, from the people at the back of the line, to the people at the front.
Once you see that, you start asking better questions. Where is new money going? Who benefits first? And what am I storing my hard work in?
So the next time you hear that new money is being created, don't just ask how much.
Ask: who gets it first?
